claim: The ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 is required for the glucose-induced internalization of Jen1.
source: We show that the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 and the glucose-regulated arrestin-related trafficking adaptors (ART) protein Rod1, involved in the glucose-induced internalization of Jen1, are also required for the post-endocytic sorting of Jen1 to the yeast lysosome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The glucose-regulated arrestin-related trafficking adaptor protein Rod1 is required for the glucose-induced internalization of Jen1.
source: We show that the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 and the glucose-regulated arrestin-related trafficking adaptors (ART) protein Rod1, involved in the glucose-induced internalization of Jen1, are also required for the post-endocytic sorting of Jen1 to the yeast lysosome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Rsp5 and Rod1 are required for the post-endocytic sorting of Jen1 to the yeast lysosome.
source: We show that the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 and the glucose-regulated arrestin-related trafficking adaptors (ART) protein Rod1, involved in the glucose-induced internalization of Jen1, are also required for the post-endocytic sorting of Jen1 to the yeast lysosome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The post-endocytic sorting step of Jen1 takes place at the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: This new step takes place at the trans-Golgi network (TGN), where Rod1 localizes dynamically upon triggering endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Rod1 localizes dynamically to the TGN upon triggering endocytosis.
source: This new step takes place at the trans-Golgi network (TGN), where Rod1 localizes dynamically upon triggering endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Transporter trafficking to the TGN after internalization is required for their degradation.
source: Indeed, transporter trafficking to the TGN after internalization is required for their degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Glucose removal promotes Rod1 relocalization to the cytosol.
source: Glucose removal promotes Rod1 relocalization to the cytosol and Jen1 deubiquitylation, allowing transporter recycling when the signal is only transient.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Glucose removal promotes Jen1 deubiquitylation.
source: Glucose removal promotes Rod1 relocalization to the cytosol and Jen1 deubiquitylation, allowing transporter recycling when the signal is only transient.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Transient glucose signals allow transporter recycling through Rod1 relocalization and Jen1 deubiquitylation.
source: Glucose removal promotes Rod1 relocalization to the cytosol and Jen1 deubiquitylation, allowing transporter recycling when the signal is only transient.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Nutrient availability regulates transporter fate through the localization of the ART/Rsp5 ubiquitylation complex at the TGN.
source: Therefore, nutrient availability regulates transporter fate through the localization of the ART/Rsp5 ubiquitylation complex at the TGN.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Ubiquitin conjugation to membrane proteins acts as a major determinant of their intracellular sorting in the endocytic pathway.
source: The conjugation of ubiquitin to membrane proteins ('cargoes') acts as a major determinant of their intracellular sorting in the endocytic pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Ubiquitin acts as a signal to promote cargo endocytosis from the plasma membrane.
source: Ubiquitin can notably act as a signal to promote cargo endocytosis from the plasma membrane (reviewed in Dupré et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Rsp5 is a conserved ubiquitin ligase of the Nedd4 family.
source: This is particularly true in yeast, and studies have shown the critical involvement of Rsp5, a conserved ubiquitin ligase of the Nedd4 family, in cargo ubiquitylation at the plasma membrane upon triggering endocytosis (reviewed in MacGurn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Rsp5 is critically involved in cargo ubiquitylation at the plasma membrane upon triggering endocytosis in yeast.
source: This is particularly true in yeast, and studies have shown the critical involvement of Rsp5, a conserved ubiquitin ligase of the Nedd4 family, in cargo ubiquitylation at the plasma membrane upon triggering endocytosis (reviewed in MacGurn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The nutritional status of the medium regulates the dynamics of cognate transporters at the plasma membrane through their regulated ubiquitylation and endocytosis.
source: Indeed, the nutritional status of the medium, such as the absence/excess of a given substrate, regulates the dynamics of the cognate transporters at the plasma membrane through their regulated ubiquitylation and endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: At the plasma membrane, the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 ubiquitylates endocytic cargoes and is assisted by adaptor proteins of the ART family.
source: Indeed, at the plasma membrane, the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 ubiquitylates endocytic cargoes and is assisted in its function by adaptor proteins of the ART family (Arrestin-Related Trafficking adaptors), that confer to Rsp5 the ability to ubiquitylate numerous transporters in response to various external inputs (Lin et al., 2008; Nikko et al., 2008; Nikko and Pelham, 2009; Hatakeyama et al., 2010; O'Donnell et al., 2010, 2013; Karachaliou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ART proteins confer to Rsp5 the ability to ubiquitylate numerous transporters in response to various external inputs.
source: Indeed, at the plasma membrane, the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 ubiquitylates endocytic cargoes and is assisted in its function by adaptor proteins of the ART family (Arrestin-Related Trafficking adaptors), that confer to Rsp5 the ability to ubiquitylate numerous transporters in response to various external inputs (Lin et al., 2008; Nikko et al., 2008; Nikko and Pelham, 2009; Hatakeyama et al., 2010; O'Donnell et al., 2010, 2013; Karachaliou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ART proteins are both targets of nutrient signaling pathways and actors of transporter ubiquitylation.
source: ART proteins are both targets of nutrient signaling pathways and actors of transporter ubiquitylation, and as such act as relay molecules allowing to coordinate transporter endocytosis with the nutrient status of the cell (MacGurn et al., 2011; Merhi and André, 2012; Becuwe et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ART proteins act as relay molecules allowing to coordinate transporter endocytosis with the nutrient status of the cell.
source: ART proteins are both targets of nutrient signaling pathways and actors of transporter ubiquitylation, and as such act as relay molecules allowing to coordinate transporter endocytosis with the nutrient status of the cell (MacGurn et al., 2011; Merhi and André, 2012; Becuwe et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The human arrestin-related protein TXNIP regulates glucose influx in cells by promoting the endocytosis of the glucose transporter GLUT1 in an AMPK-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, the human arrestin-related protein TXNIP was recently reported to regulate glucose influx in cells by promoting the endocytosis of the glucose transporter GLUT1 in an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent manner, illustrating the conservation of arrestin-related proteins function in endocytosis (Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The function of arrestin-related proteins in endocytosis is conserved from yeast to humans.
source: Interestingly, the human arrestin-related protein TXNIP was recently reported to regulate glucose influx in cells by promoting the endocytosis of the glucose transporter GLUT1 in an AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent manner, illustrating the conservation of arrestin-related proteins function in endocytosis (Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and inference from the comparison between yeast and human systems.

claim: In mammalian cells, cargo ubiquitylation often occurs at the plasma membrane.
source: In mammalian cells, cargo ubiquitylation often occurs at the plasma membrane, and in some cases, this is essential for internalization, as demonstrated for the sodium channel ENaC (Zhou et al., 2007) or the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I (Hewitt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Ubiquitylation at the plasma membrane is essential for internalization of the sodium channel ENaC.
source: In mammalian cells, cargo ubiquitylation often occurs at the plasma membrane, and in some cases, this is essential for internalization, as demonstrated for the sodium channel ENaC (Zhou et al., 2007) or the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I (Hewitt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Ubiquitylation at the plasma membrane is essential for internalization of the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I.
source: In mammalian cells, cargo ubiquitylation often occurs at the plasma membrane, and in some cases, this is essential for internalization, as demonstrated for the sodium channel ENaC (Zhou et al., 2007) or the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) class I (Hewitt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Affecting the ubiquitylation of β2-AR does not abrogate its internalization.
source: However, this is not a general rule, because affecting the ubiquitylation of the G-protein-coupled receptors β2-AR and CXCR4 (Shenoy et al., 2001; Marchese and Benovic, 2001 #885), or the receptor tyrosine kinases EGFR and FGFR-1 (Huang et al., 2006; Haugsten et al., 2008) does not abrogate their internalization.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Affecting the ubiquitylation of CXCR4 does not abrogate its internalization.
source: However, this is not a general rule, because affecting the ubiquitylation of the G-protein-coupled receptors β2-AR and CXCR4 (Shenoy et al., 2001; Marchese and Benovic, 2001 #885), or the receptor tyrosine kinases EGFR and FGFR-1 (Huang et al., 2006; Haugsten et al., 2008) does not abrogate their internalization.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Affecting the ubiquitylation of EGFR does not abrogate its internalization.
source: However, this is not a general rule, because affecting the ubiquitylation of the G-protein-coupled receptors β2-AR and CXCR4 (Shenoy et al., 2001; Marchese and Benovic, 2001 #885), or the receptor tyrosine kinases EGFR and FGFR-1 (Huang et al., 2006; Haugsten et al., 2008) does not abrogate their internalization.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Affecting the ubiquitylation of FGFR-1 does not abrogate its internalization.
source: However, this is not a general rule, because affecting the ubiquitylation of the G-protein-coupled receptors β2-AR and CXCR4 (Shenoy et al., 2001; Marchese and Benovic, 2001 #885), or the receptor tyrosine kinases EGFR and FGFR-1 (Huang et al., 2006; Haugsten et al., 2008) does not abrogate their internalization.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Cargo ubiquitylation becomes critical later in the endocytic pathway to promote cargo sorting towards late endosomes and their subsequent degradation.
source: Instead, cargo ubiquitylation becomes critical later in the endocytic pathway, to promote cargo sorting towards late endosomes and their subsequent degradation (see for instance Miranda et al., 2007; Kabra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: At endosomes, ubiquitinated cargoes are captured and sorted by ESCRT proteins into the lumen of the endosome through multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis.
source: At endosomes, ubiquitinated cargoes are captured and sorted by ESCRT proteins (Endosomal Sorting Complex Required For Transport) into the lumen of the endosome through a process known as multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis (MacGurn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Loss of cargo ubiquitylation leads to cargo recycling to the cell surface.
source: Loss of cargo ubiquitylation reportedly leads to their recycling to the cell surface (Shenoy et al., 2001; Huang et al., 2006; Haugsten et al., 2008; Eden et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A major function of ubiquitin conjugation to endocytic cargoes is to regulate their post-endocytic fate.
source: Therefore, a major function of ubiquitin conjugation to endocytic cargoes is to regulate their post-endocytic fate.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the cited literature.

claim: The competition between ubiquitylation and deubiquitylation at endosomes can decide the fate of many endocytosed cargoes.
source: Because ubiquitylation is a reversible modification, the competition between ubiquitylation and deubiquitylation at endosomes can decide the fate of many of the endocytosed cargoes, as only proteins that are stably ubiquitylated will be ultimately degraded.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference based on the reversibility of ubiquitylation.

claim: Only proteins that are stably ubiquitylated will be ultimately degraded.
source: Because ubiquitylation is a reversible modification, the competition between ubiquitylation and deubiquitylation at endosomes can decide the fate of many of the endocytosed cargoes, as only proteins that are stably ubiquitylated will be ultimately degraded.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference.

claim: Several deubiquitylating enzymes control the recycling of endosomal cargoes such as EGFR in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, several deubiquitylating enzymes were indeed shown to control the recycling of endosomal cargoes such as EGFR (McCullough et al., 2004; Mizuno et al., 2005; Row et al., 2006), the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator (CFTR) (Bomberger et al., 2009), ENaC (Butterworth et al., 2007) or the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2-AR) (Berthouze et al., 2009) (reviewed in Clague et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several deubiquitylating enzymes control the recycling of CFTR in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, several deubiquitylating enzymes were indeed shown to control the recycling of endosomal cargoes such as EGFR (McCullough et al., 2004; Mizuno et al., 2005; Row et al., 2006), the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator (CFTR) (Bomberger et al., 2009), ENaC (Butterworth et al., 2007) or the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2-AR) (Berthouze et al., 2009) (reviewed in Clague et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Several deubiquitylating enzymes control the recycling of ENaC in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, several deubiquitylating enzymes were indeed shown to control the recycling of endosomal cargoes such as EGFR (McCullough et al., 2004; Mizuno et al., 2005; Row et al., 2006), the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator (CFTR) (Bomberger et al., 2009), ENaC (Butterworth et al., 2007) or the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2-AR) (Berthouze et al., 2009) (reviewed in Clague et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Several deubiquitylating enzymes control the recycling of β2-AR in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, several deubiquitylating enzymes were indeed shown to control the recycling of endosomal cargoes such as EGFR (McCullough et al., 2004; Mizuno et al., 2005; Row et al., 2006), the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Regulator (CFTR) (Bomberger et al., 2009), ENaC (Butterworth et al., 2007) or the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2-AR) (Berthouze et al., 2009) (reviewed in Clague et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The mechanisms by which external signals are integrated and transduced to the ubiquitylation machinery to regulate cargo trafficking are unknown.
source: However, the mechanisms by which external signals are integrated and transduced to the ubiquitylation machinery in order to regulate cargo trafficking are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Glucose triggers the endocytosis of various yeast carbon sources transporters.
source: We recently reported that glucose, which triggers the endocytosis of various yeast carbon sources transporters (reviewed in Horak, 2013), promotes the successive dephosphorylation and ubiquitylation of the ART protein Rod1 (also known as Art4), leading to its activation (Becuwe et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Glucose promotes the successive dephosphorylation and ubiquitylation of the ART protein Rod1, leading to its activation.
source: We recently reported that glucose, which triggers the endocytosis of various yeast carbon sources transporters (reviewed in Horak, 2013), promotes the successive dephosphorylation and ubiquitylation of the ART protein Rod1 (also known as Art4), leading to its activation (Becuwe et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Activated Rod1 promotes the glucose-induced ubiquitylation and degradation of Jen1.
source: In turn, activated Rod1 promotes the glucose-induced ubiquitylation and degradation of Jen1, a monocarboxylate transporter.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous work.

claim: The place where Rod1 regulates endocytosis is unknown.
source: However, the place where Rod1 regulates endocytosis is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: There are conflicting reports regarding the step at which ART proteins control intracellular trafficking.
source: Whereas ART proteins are considered to promote transporter internalization (Becuwe et al., 2012a), there are conflicting reports regarding the step at which they control intracellular trafficking (Helliwell et al., 2001; Soetens et al., 2001; Merhi and André, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting studies.

claim: ART proteins were observed at various subcellular locations, both in yeast and mammalian cells.
source: Moreover, ART proteins were observed at various subcellular locations, both in yeast (Lin et al., 2008; O'Donnell et al., 2010) and mammalian cells (Vina-Vilaseca et al., 2011; Han et al., 2013) suggesting other roles beyond the regulation of cargo internalization.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The yeast iron transporter complex Fet3/Ftr1 is internalized independently of its ubiquitylation.
source: Furthermore, it was reported that akin to the situation in mammalian cells, the yeast iron transporter complex Fet3/Ftr1 is internalized independently of its ubiquitylation, although the latter is required for its vacuolar targeting.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Ubiquitylation of Fet3/Ftr1 is required for its vacuolar targeting.
source: Furthermore, it was reported that akin to the situation in mammalian cells, the yeast iron transporter complex Fet3/Ftr1 is internalized independently of its ubiquitylation, although the latter is required for its vacuolar targeting.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The molecular actors involved in post-endocytic ubiquitylation of Fet3/Ftr1 are not known.
source: This suggests a control of transporter degradation through a post-endocytic ubiquitylation event, for which the molecular actors are not known (Strochlic et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap and supported by a citation.

claim: Rod1 has a dual function in transporter sorting at the plasma membrane and at a post-endocytic compartment.
source: Here, through the use of microfluidics-assisted live-cell imaging, we studied the place of action of Rod1 during endocytosis and report a dual function of Rod1 in transporter sorting at two successive locations in the cell, that is, at the plasma membrane to control transporter internalization, and at a post-endocytic compartment to promote vacuolar sorting and degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding in the introduction.

claim: Rod1 is required for the glucose-induced endocytosis and degradation of Stl1.
source: The glucose-induced endocytosis and degradation of Stl1 required Rod1, establishing Stl1 as a new Rod1-regulated cargo (Figure 1A,B), in addition to the previously described hexose transporter Hxt6 (Nikko and Pelham, 2009) and Jen1 (Becuwe et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Stl1 is a new Rod1-regulated cargo.
source: The glucose-induced endocytosis and degradation of Stl1 required Rod1, establishing Stl1 as a new Rod1-regulated cargo (Figure 1A,B), in addition to the previously described hexose transporter Hxt6 (Nikko and Pelham, 2009) and Jen1 (Becuwe et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1A,B and supported by citations to previous work on other cargoes.

claim: Stl1-GFP was internalized within 5 min after glucose addition in WT cells.
source: Whereas Stl1-GFP was internalized within 5 min after glucose addition in WT cells, it remained stably associated to the plasma membrane in the rod1Δ mutant and was not internalized even 30 min after glucose treatment (Figure 1C, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Stl1-GFP remained stably associated to the plasma membrane in the rod1Δ mutant and was not internalized even 30 min after glucose treatment.
source: Whereas Stl1-GFP was internalized within 5 min after glucose addition in WT cells, it remained stably associated to the plasma membrane in the rod1Δ mutant and was not internalized even 30 min after glucose treatment (Figure 1C, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Rod1 has a canonical role in transporter internalization at the plasma membrane.
source: This is in agreement with a canonical role of Rod1 in transporter internalization at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the Stl1 data.

claim: Glucose triggered the transient localization of Jen1 to cytoplasmic puncta in rod1Δ cells.
source: Then, we monitored the trafficking of the monocarboxylate transporter Jen1-GFP in rod1Δ cells after glucose addition. We observed that, in sharp contrast with the result obtained for Stl1 (see Figure 1C), glucose triggered the transient localization of Jen1 to cytoplasmic puncta (Figure 1D, Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1D and Video 2.

claim: The appearance of Jen1-positive puncta in rod1Δ cells was strongly affected by latrunculin A treatment.
source: The appearance of these puncta was strongly affected by latrunculin A treatment, which disrupts the actin cytoskeleton and abolishes endocytosis, indicative of their endocytic origin (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Jen1 was still internalized in the rod1Δ mutant.
source: This showed that Jen1 was still internalized in the rod1Δ mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the latrunculin A experiment.

claim: The appearance of Jen1-positive vesicles was delayed in the rod1Δ mutant as compared to the wild type.
source: First, we observed that the appearance of Jen1-positive vesicles was delayed in the rod1Δ mutant as compared to the wild type (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In the absence of Rod1, Jen1 internalization still occurred but was less efficient.
source: This clearly showed that in the absence of Rod1, Jen1 internalization still occurred but was less efficient, which was also supported by the persistence of a Jen1-GFP pool at the plasma membrane in the rod1Δ strain.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the quantitative data.

claim: Jen1-GFP was targeted into larger and brighter structures (likely late endosomes) at later time points in the WT.
source: A second observation was that whereas Jen1-GFP was targeted into larger and brighter structures (likely to be late endosomes) at later time points in the WT, it did not reach this compartment in the rod1Δ mutant (Figure 1F, Video 3) but rather re-localized to the plasma membrane, as described previously (Becuwe et al., 2012b) (see also Figure 1D and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1F and Video 3.

claim: Jen1-GFP did not reach late endosomes in the rod1Δ mutant but rather re-localized to the plasma membrane.
source: A second observation was that whereas Jen1-GFP was targeted into larger and brighter structures (likely to be late endosomes) at later time points in the WT, it did not reach this compartment in the rod1Δ mutant (Figure 1F, Video 3) but rather re-localized to the plasma membrane, as described previously (Becuwe et al., 2012b) (see also Figure 1D and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1F and Video 3, and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The plasma membrane-localized pool of Jen1 in rod1Δ cells did not originate from de novo Jen1 synthesis.
source: Because JEN1 expression is repressed by glucose (Bojunga and Entian, 1999), this plasma membrane-localized pool did not originate from de novo Jen1 synthesis, but rather from the recycling of internalized Jen1 back to the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the known repression of JEN1 by glucose, supported by a citation.

claim: The plasma membrane-localized pool of Jen1 in rod1Δ cells originated from the recycling of internalized Jen1 back to the cell surface.
source: Because JEN1 expression is repressed by glucose (Bojunga and Entian, 1999), this plasma membrane-localized pool did not originate from de novo Jen1 synthesis, but rather from the recycling of internalized Jen1 back to the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the known repression of JEN1 by glucose.

claim: Rod1 has a role in the post-endocytic targeting of Jen1 to the vacuole, in addition to its function at the plasma membrane.
source: This result strongly suggested a role for Rod1 in the post-endocytic targeting of Jen1 to the vacuole, in addition to its function at the plasma membrane (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the Jen1 trafficking data.

claim: Rod1 is required for an efficient glucose-induced ubiquitylation of Jen1.
source: Because we previously showed that Rod1 is required for an efficient glucose-induced ubiquitylation of Jen1 (Becuwe et al., 2012b), the observation that Jen1 can be partially internalized in the absence of Rod1 led us to investigate whether this endocytosis still relies on Jen1 ubiquitylation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The remnant internalization of Jen1 observed in the rod1Δ mutant still required its ubiquitylation.
source: Indeed, the remnant internalization of Jen1 observed in the rod1Δ mutant still required its ubiquitylation, as demonstrated through the use of a non-ubiquitylatable Jen1 mutant in which all cytosolic lysine residues have been mutated into arginine residues (Jen1-KR-GFP, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data using the Jen1-KR mutant shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mutations of all cytosolic lysine residues to arginine in Jen1 abolished Jen1 ubiquitylation in response to glucose.
source: As expected, these mutations abolished Jen1 ubiquitylation in response to glucose (Figure 2B), but this construct was still functional, as judged by its ability to transport selenite, that can be used as a readout for Jen1 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (McDermott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Jen1-KR construct was still functional, as judged by its ability to transport selenite.
source: As expected, these mutations abolished Jen1 ubiquitylation in response to glucose (Figure 2B), but this construct was still functional, as judged by its ability to transport selenite, that can be used as a readout for Jen1 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (McDermott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and supported by a citation.

claim: Jen1-KR-GFP was targeted to the plasma membrane, although it displayed a small delay in secretion as observed by its transient accumulation at the ER.
source: The visualization of the subcellular localization of Jen1-KR-GFP showed that it was indeed targeted to the plasma membrane, although it displayed a small delay in secretion as observed by its transient accumulation at the ER (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The endocytosis of Jen1-KR-GFP in response to glucose was abolished.
source: More importantly, the endocytosis of Jen1-KR-GFP in response to glucose was abolished (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Jen1 can be ubiquitylated at the plasma membrane independently of Rod1, at least when Rod1 is absent.
source: Since Jen1 was partially endocytosed in the absence of Rod1 (see Figure 1D,F,G), we conclude that Jen1 can be ubiquitylated at the plasma membrane independently of Rod1, at least when Rod1 is absent.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the Jen1-KR data.

claim: There are additional ubiquitylation systems besides Rod1 at the plasma membrane that can promote Jen1 internalization.
source: Consequently, it is likely that there are additional ubiquitylation systems besides Rod1 at the plasma membrane, which can promote Jen1 internalization and that remain to be identified.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the data.

claim: Jen1 was still internalized in the multiple 9-arrestin mutant.
source: Of note, Jen1 was still internalized in the multiple 9-arrestin mutant (Figure 2D), which lacks Rod1 and eight other arrestin-related proteins (Nikko and Pelham, 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 2D and supported by a citation.

claim: The function of Rod1 at the plasma membrane is either compensated or is redundant with other adaptors.
source: Altogether, these results show that the function of Rod1 at the plasma membrane is either compensated or is redundant with other adaptors, but that this is not the case regarding its post-endocytic function in Jen1 trafficking.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data on Jen1 internalization in various mutants.

claim: The post-endocytic function of Rod1 in Jen1 trafficking is not compensated or redundant with other adaptors.
source: Altogether, these results show that the function of Rod1 at the plasma membrane is either compensated or is redundant with other adaptors, but that this is not the case regarding its post-endocytic function in Jen1 trafficking.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Rod1-GFP appeared as a diffuse cytosolic protein in lactate-grown cells.
source: Rod1-GFP appeared as a diffuse cytosolic protein in lactate-grown cells that transiently localized to punctate structures upon glucose stimulation (Figure 3A, Video 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3A and Video 4.

claim: Rod1-GFP transiently localized to punctate structures upon glucose stimulation.
source: Rod1-GFP appeared as a diffuse cytosolic protein in lactate-grown cells that transiently localized to punctate structures upon glucose stimulation (Figure 3A, Video 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3A and Video 4.

claim: Rod1 localization to punctate structures was due to the recruitment of pre-existing Rod1 to these puncta.
source: This localization was due to the recruitment of pre-existing Rod1 to these puncta, because inhibition of translation with cycloheximide did not affect this localization (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3B using cycloheximide treatment.

claim: Rod1-positive puncta did not originate from the plasma membrane by endocytosis.
source: Also, these puncta did not originate from the plasma membrane by endocytosis because Rod1 behaved similarly when endocytosis was abolished by latrunculin A treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3C using latrunculin A treatment.

claim: Rod1-positive puncta co-localized with Sec7-mCh, a marker of the TGN.
source: Instead, these puncta co-localized with Sec7-mCh (Figure 3D, Video 5), a marker of the TGN (trans-Golgi network) (Franzusoff et al., 1991), indicating that Rod1 transiently localizes to the TGN in response to glucose.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3D and Video 5, and supported by a citation for Sec7 as a TGN marker.

claim: Rod1 transiently localizes to the TGN in response to glucose.
source: Instead, these puncta co-localized with Sec7-mCh (Figure 3D, Video 5), a marker of the TGN (trans-Golgi network) (Franzusoff et al., 1991), indicating that Rod1 transiently localizes to the TGN in response to glucose.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3D and Video 5.

claim: Deletion of REG1 abolished Rod1 targeting to the TGN.
source: Deletion of REG1, encoding a subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) required for Rod1 activation (Becuwe et al., 2012b), abolished Rod1 targeting to the TGN, demonstrating that Rod1 localization to the TGN was a consequence of its glucose-induced activation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3E and supported by a citation.

claim: Rod1 localization to the TGN was a consequence of its glucose-induced activation.
source: Deletion of REG1, encoding a subunit of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) required for Rod1 activation (Becuwe et al., 2012b), abolished Rod1 targeting to the TGN, demonstrating that Rod1 localization to the TGN was a consequence of its glucose-induced activation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the reg1Δ experiment.

claim: Early after glucose treatment, the Jen1-GFP puncta co-localized nearly exclusively with Vps17-mCh.
source: Early after glucose treatment, the Jen1-GFP puncta co-localized nearly exclusively with Vps17-mCh, but this was followed by a partial co-localization with Sec7-mCh (Figure 4A,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Video 6), showing that Jen1-GFP associates with the TGN after internalization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4A,C and related figures/videos.

claim: Jen1-GFP co-localization with Vps17-mCh was followed by a partial co-localization with Sec7-mCh.
source: Early after glucose treatment, the Jen1-GFP puncta co-localized nearly exclusively with Vps17-mCh, but this was followed by a partial co-localization with Sec7-mCh (Figure 4A,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Video 6), showing that Jen1-GFP associates with the TGN after internalization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4A,C and related figures/videos.

claim: Jen1-GFP associates with the TGN after internalization.
source: Early after glucose treatment, the Jen1-GFP puncta co-localized nearly exclusively with Vps17-mCh, but this was followed by a partial co-localization with Sec7-mCh (Figure 4A,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Video 6), showing that Jen1-GFP associates with the TGN after internalization.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the co-localization data.

claim: In the rod1Δ mutant, Jen1-GFP followed essentially the same route as in WT cells, although Jen1-GFP displayed a prolonged co-localization with Sec7-mCh.
source: The same co-localization analysis was carried out in the rod1Δ mutant, and revealed that Jen1-GFP followed essentially the same route as in WT cells, although Jen1-GFP displayed a prolonged co-localization with Sec7-mCh (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplements 4, 5, Video 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4B,C and related figures/videos.

claim: Jen1 transiently accumulates at the TGN in the absence of Rod1.
source: Therefore, Jen1 not only traffics to the TGN after internalization before it reaches the vacuole in wild-type cells, but also transiently accumulates at this compartment in the absence of Rod1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the co-localization data in rod1Δ cells.

claim: In the vps52Δ strain, Jen1 was internalized but accumulated into cytoplasmic puncta and failed to reach the vacuole.
source: In this strain, Jen1 was internalized but accumulated into cytoplasmic puncta and failed to reach the vacuole (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Similar results were obtained in mutants for the yeast Rab6 homologue, ypt6Δ, or for components of its GEF, rgp1Δ and ric1Δ.
source: Similar results were obtained in other mutants affected in retrograde trafficking, such as mutants for the yeast Rab6 homologue, ypt6Δ, or for components of its GEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor), rgp1Δ and ric1Δ (Siniossoglou et al., 2000) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4E and supported by a citation.

claim: Jen1 degradation was strongly affected in retrograde mutants upon glucose treatment.
source: Moreover, Jen1 degradation was strongly affected in these retrograde mutants upon glucose treatment (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the ypt6Δ mutant, Jen1 no longer co-localized with the TGN.
source: As expected, in the ypt6Δ mutant, Jen1 no longer co-localized with the TGN (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Endosome-to-TGN trafficking is critical for the vacuolar sorting of Jen1 after its internalization.
source: Therefore, these data reveal that endosome-to-TGN trafficking is critical for the vacuolar sorting of Jen1 after its internalization, suggesting that a step in the post-endocytic of Jen1 occurs at the TGN, prior to its delivery to the vacuole.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the retrograde mutant data.

claim: A step in the post-endocytic trafficking of Jen1 occurs at the TGN, prior to its delivery to the vacuole.
source: Therefore, these data reveal that endosome-to-TGN trafficking is critical for the vacuolar sorting of Jen1 after its internalization, suggesting that a step in the post-endocytic of Jen1 occurs at the TGN, prior to its delivery to the vacuole.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the retrograde mutant data.

claim: The absence of the Gga1/Gga2 proteins did not reduce Jen1 internalization, but partially impaired its vacuolar targeting, leading to Jen1 recycling at the plasma membrane.
source: As shown in Figure 4H, the absence of the Gga1/Gga2 proteins did not reduce Jen1 internalization, but partially impaired its vacuolar targeting, leading to Jen1 recycling at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Jen1-GFP co-localized more strongly with the TGN marker, Sec7-mCh, after endocytosis in the gga1Δ gga2Δ mutant than in WT cells.
source: Of note, Jen1-GFP co-localized more strongly with the TGN marker, Sec7-mCh, after endocytosis in the gga1Δ gga2Δ mutant than in WT cells (Figure 4H,I), thus mimicking the defects observed in the rod1Δ mutant (Figure 1 and Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: TGN-to-endosome sorting is critical for the post-endocytic targeting of Jen1 to the vacuole.
source: These results showed that TGN-to-endosome sorting is also critical for the post-endocytic targeting of Jen1 to the vacuole.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the gga1Δ gga2Δ mutant data.

claim: The dicarboxylic amino acid transporter Dip5 transiently co-localizes with the TGN during its substrate-induced endocytosis.
source: Of note, we also obtained evidence that another transporter, the dicarboxylic amino acid transporter Dip5, also transiently co-localizes with the TGN during its substrate-induced endocytosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 8), and that its vacuolar sorting also depends on the Gga1/Gga2 proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: The vacuolar sorting of Dip5 depends on the Gga1/Gga2 proteins.
source: Of note, we also obtained evidence that another transporter, the dicarboxylic amino acid transporter Dip5, also transiently co-localizes with the TGN during its substrate-induced endocytosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 8), and that its vacuolar sorting also depends on the Gga1/Gga2 proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9.

claim: The post-endocytic control of transporter fate at the TGN is not restricted to Jen1 but is likely to be a more general mechanism.
source: Therefore, the post-endocytic control of transporter fate at the TGN is not restricted to Jen1 but is likely to be a more general mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the Dip5 data.

claim: In the vps52Δ mutant, in which Jen1 departs from the plasma membrane in response to glucose but cannot reach the TGN, there was a sharp decrease in Jen1 ubiquitylation after 20 min of glucose treatment.
source: Indeed, in the vps52Δ mutant, in which Jen1 departs from the plasma membrane in response to glucose but cannot reach the TGN, we observed a sharp decrease in Jen1 ubiquitylation after 20 min of glucose treatment (Figure 5A; see also Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 4F.

claim: The progressive loss of Jen1 ubiquitylated species was likely due to a deubiquitylation event occurring during the progression of Jen1 from the plasma membrane to the TGN.
source: Because Jen1 expression is repressed by glucose (Bojunga and Entian, 1999), the progressive loss of Jen1 ubiquitylated species was likely due to a deubiquitylation event occurring during the progression of Jen1 from the plasma membrane to the TGN.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the known repression of JEN1 by glucose, supported by a citation.

claim: In the vrp1Δ mutant, Jen1 displayed a robust ubiquitylation pattern, indicating that the disappearance of Jen1 ubiquitylated species was not due to an intrinsic lability of ubiquitin-conjugated Jen1.
source: We then performed the same experiment in a vrp1Δ (end5Δ) mutant, in which endocytosis is blocked due to the deletion of the gene encoding the yeast WASP-interacting protein (WIP) homologue, verprolin (Munn et al., 1995). In this mutant, however, Jen1 displayed a robust ubiquitylation pattern, indicating that the disappearance of Jen1 ubiquitylated species was not due to an intrinsic lability of ubiquitin-conjugated Jen1, and that this remodeling occurred post-internalization (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 5A and supported by a citation.

claim: The remodeling of Jen1 ubiquitylation occurred post-internalization.
source: We then performed the same experiment in a vrp1Δ (end5Δ) mutant, in which endocytosis is blocked due to the deletion of the gene encoding the yeast WASP-interacting protein (WIP) homologue, verprolin (Munn et al., 1995). In this mutant, however, Jen1 displayed a robust ubiquitylation pattern, indicating that the disappearance of Jen1 ubiquitylated species was not due to an intrinsic lability of ubiquitin-conjugated Jen1, and that this remodeling occurred post-internalization (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the vrp1Δ mutant data.

claim: In the gga1Δgga2Δ strain, in which Jen1 transiently accumulates at the TGN, Jen1 also accumulated in an ubiquitylated state.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we observed that in the gga1Δgga2Δ strain, in which Jen1 transiently accumulates at the TGN (see Figure 4H,I), Jen1 also accumulated in an ubiquitylated state, suggesting that retaining Jen1 at the TGN leads to its massive ubiquitylation (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Retaining Jen1 at the TGN leads to its massive ubiquitylation.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we observed that in the gga1Δgga2Δ strain, in which Jen1 transiently accumulates at the TGN (see Figure 4H,I), Jen1 also accumulated in an ubiquitylated state, suggesting that retaining Jen1 at the TGN leads to its massive ubiquitylation (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: In the triple ypt6Δ gga1Δ gga2Δ mutant, Jen1 ubiquitylation was similar to that observed in a single ypt6Δ mutant.
source: To confirm that this was due to the ubiquitylation of Jen1 molecules originating from endosomes, we used a triple ypt6Δ gga1Δ gga2Δ mutant in which retrograde trafficking is abolished. In this mutant, Jen1 ubiquitylation was similar to that observed in a single ypt6Δ mutant, showing that the accumulation of ubiquitylated species of Jen1 at the TGN observed in the gga1Δ gga2Δ mutants indeed required retrograde trafficking (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The accumulation of ubiquitylated species of Jen1 at the TGN observed in the gga1Δ gga2Δ mutants required retrograde trafficking.
source: To confirm that this was due to the ubiquitylation of Jen1 molecules originating from endosomes, we used a triple ypt6Δ gga1Δ gga2Δ mutant in which retrograde trafficking is abolished. In this mutant, Jen1 ubiquitylation was similar to that observed in a single ypt6Δ mutant, showing that the accumulation of ubiquitylated species of Jen1 at the TGN observed in the gga1Δ gga2Δ mutants indeed required retrograde trafficking (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the triple mutant data.

claim: A glucose-induced recruitment of the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 to the TGN was observed in response to glucose.
source: In further support of an ubiquitylation event occurring at the TGN, we also observed a glucose-induced recruitment of the ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 to this compartment in response to glucose (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Rsp5 co-localizes with Jen1 at the TGN.
source: Using three-color imaging, we also showed a co-localization of Rsp5 with Jen1 and Rod1 at the TGN (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Rsp5 co-localizes with Rod1 at the TGN.
source: Using three-color imaging, we also showed a co-localization of Rsp5 with Jen1 and Rod1 at the TGN (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Jen1 is ubiquitylated at the plasma membrane and is deubiquitylated after its internalization.
source: Altogether, these data strongly suggest that Jen1 is ubiquitylated at the plasma membrane and is deubiquitylated after its internalization, and lead us to propose that a second, glucose-regulated ubiquitylation step at the TGN involving Rsp5 and Rod1 may control Jen1 progression from the TGN to the vacuole.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the ubiquitylation dynamics data.

claim: A second, glucose-regulated ubiquitylation step at the TGN involving Rsp5 and Rod1 may control Jen1 progression from the TGN to the vacuole.
source: Altogether, these data strongly suggest that Jen1 is ubiquitylated at the plasma membrane and is deubiquitylated after its internalization, and lead us to propose that a second, glucose-regulated ubiquitylation step at the TGN involving Rsp5 and Rod1 may control Jen1 progression from the TGN to the vacuole.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed model based on the data.

claim: A short pulse of glucose (10 min) was sufficient to drive Jen1-GFP internalization.
source: To test this prediction, we treated lactate-grown cells expressing Jen1-GFP with a short pulse of glucose (10 min), which was sufficient to drive Jen1-GFP internalization, and then followed Jen1-GFP trafficking upon glucose removal.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Jen1 redistributed back to the plasma membrane within 20 min upon glucose removal.
source: Using this protocol, Jen1 redistributed back to the plasma membrane within 20 min (Figure 6A), showing that Jen1 endocytosis was reversible upon glucose removal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Jen1 endocytosis was reversible upon glucose removal.
source: Using this protocol, Jen1 redistributed back to the plasma membrane within 20 min (Figure 6A), showing that Jen1 endocytosis was reversible upon glucose removal.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the glucose removal experiment.

claim: Jen1 relocalization to the plasma membrane upon glucose removal coincided with a loss of Jen1 ubiquitylation.
source: This change in localization coincided with a loss of Jen1 ubiquitylation, suggesting that a continuous presence of glucose is required for the persistent ubiquitylation of Jen1 and its degradation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A continuous presence of glucose is required for the persistent ubiquitylation of Jen1 and its degradation.
source: This change in localization coincided with a loss of Jen1 ubiquitylation, suggesting that a continuous presence of glucose is required for the persistent ubiquitylation of Jen1 and its degradation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Jen1 deubiquitylation upon glucose removal is not due to Jen1 degradation but to a rapid deubiquitylation event.
source: The same experiment performed in the vrp1Δ mutant, in which endocytosis is blocked, also led to a loss of Jen1 ubiquitylation, showing it is not due to Jen1 degradation but rather to a rapid deubiquitylation event following glucose removal, regardless of Jen1 localization (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6B using the vrp1Δ mutant.

claim: Jen1 no longer recycled to the plasma membrane in the vps52Δ strain upon glucose removal.
source: Of note, Jen1 no longer recycled to the plasma membrane in the vps52Δ strain in these conditions (Figure 6C and Video 8), indicating that Jen1 recycling requires a functional endosome-to-TGN retrograde pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6C and Video 8.

claim: Jen1 recycling requires a functional endosome-to-TGN retrograde pathway.
source: Of note, Jen1 no longer recycled to the plasma membrane in the vps52Δ strain in these conditions (Figure 6C and Video 8), indicating that Jen1 recycling requires a functional endosome-to-TGN retrograde pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the vps52Δ mutant data.

claim: Jen1 recycling led to its polarized redistribution to the cell buds.
source: Therefore, a second, glucose-based sorting event occurs after internalization and takes place at the TGN. Accordingly, Jen1 recycling led to its polarized redistribution to the cell buds (Figure 6C and Video 8), similarly to the exocytic SNARE Snc1 and the chitin synthase Chs3, which localize to the cell membrane in a polarized fashion after endocytosis and recycling through the TGN (Holthuis et al., 1998; Lewis et al., 2000).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6C and Video 8, and supported by citations to similar observations for other proteins.

claim: Jen1 recycling to the cell membrane upon glucose removal correlated with the loss of Rod1 localization at the TGN.
source: Interestingly, Jen1 recycling to the cell membrane upon glucose removal also correlated with the loss of Rod1 localization at the TGN (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Rod1 localization was extremely responsive to glucose treatments.
source: Rod1 localization was indeed extremely responsive to glucose treatments, and applying repeated glucose/lactate cycles revealed a robust sensor-like response of Rod1 regarding its localization (Figure 6D and Video 9) and post-translational modifications (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6D and Video 9.

claim: Applying repeated glucose/lactate cycles revealed a robust sensor-like response of Rod1 regarding its post-translational modifications.
source: Rod1 localization was indeed extremely responsive to glucose treatments, and applying repeated glucose/lactate cycles revealed a robust sensor-like response of Rod1 regarding its localization (Figure 6D and Video 9) and post-translational modifications (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Jen1 ubiquitylation and endocytosis can be re-evaluated at the TGN after internalization upon disappearance of the endocytic stimulus.
source: Therefore, Jen1 ubiquitylation and endocytosis can be re-evaluated at the TGN after internalization upon disappearance of the endocytic stimulus, and this correlates with a rapid glucose-induced remodeling of Rod1 post-translational modifications and its redistribution from the TGN to the cytosol.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the glucose removal experiments.

claim: The glucose-induced recruitment of Rod1 and Rsp5 to the TGN promotes Jen1 ubiquitylation and its exit from the TGN to the vacuole in a Gga1-Gga2 dependent manner.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the observed glucose-induced recruitment of Rod1 and Rsp5 to the TGN promotes Jen1 ubiquitylation and its exit from the TGN to the vacuole in a Gga1-Gga2 dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data on neosynthesized Jen1 sorting.

claim: Rod1 is required for the glucose-induced retargeting of Jen1 from the secretory pathway to the vacuole.
source: We observed that the addition of glucose perturbed Jen1 sorting in the secretory pathway, as Jen1 was targeted to the vacuole instead of the plasma membrane in WT cells (Figure 7B, Video 10). This localization did not involve Jen1 targeting to the plasma membrane and its endocytosis, because Jen1 behaved similarly in the endocytic mutant vrp1Δ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). In the rod1Δ mutant, however, Jen1 was no longer targeted to the vacuole, but instead reached the cell surface (Figure 7B, Video 10), showing that Rod1 is required to divert Jen1 trafficking from the secretory pathway to the vacuole.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 7B and Video 10.

claim: Jen1 ubiquitylation is critical for its rerouting from the secretory pathway to the vacuolar pathway.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, a non-ubiquitylatable Jen1-KR-GFP construct (see Figure 2) was targeted to the plasma membrane despite the presence of glucose (Figure 7D), showing that Jen1 ubiquitylation is critical for its rerouting from the secretory pathway to the vacuolar pathway.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The vacuolar sorting of neosynthesized Jen1 from the TGN to the vacuole involved Rsp5.
source: A similar result was obtained in a hypomorphic mutant of RSP5, npi1, showing that the vacuolar sorting of neosynthesized Jen1 from the TGN to the vacuole also involved Rsp5 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Deletion of the genes encoding the ubiquitin-binding, clathrin adaptor proteins Gga1 and Gga2 led to a defect in the vacuolar targeting of neosynthesized Jen1 in the presence of glucose.
source: Furthermore, deletion of the genes encoding the ubiquitin-binding, clathrin adaptor proteins Gga1 and Gga2 proteins also led to a defect in the vacuolar targeting of neosynthesized Jen1 in the presence of glucose (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The use of microfluidics-assisted live cell imaging allowed following the dynamics of cargo trafficking in response to variations in the presence of the endocytic stimulus.
source: In the present study, the use of microfluidics-assisted live cell imaging allowed us to follow, for the first time, the dynamics of cargo trafficking in response to variations in the presence of the endocytic stimulus, as well as the localization of the ART protein Rod1 in these conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a methodological contribution.

claim: Rod1 exerts a function at the plasma membrane, as it is essential for the endocytosis of Stl1, and required for the efficient internalization of Jen1 upon glucose treatment.
source: This revealed a dual function of the ART protein Rod1 in the control of transporter endocytosis and degradation by glucose availability (Figure 8, left and middle panel). First, Rod1 exerts a function at the plasma membrane, as it is essential for the endocytosis of the glycerol/proton symporter Stl1, and required for the efficient internalization of Jen1 upon glucose treatment (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings in the discussion.

claim: Rod1 controls transporter sorting after endocytosis, a step which takes place at the trans-Golgi network.
source: Second, Rod1 also controls transporter sorting after endocytosis, a step which takes place at the trans-Golgi network (Figure 8, middle panel).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings in the discussion.

claim: Both the endosome-to-Golgi retrograde pathway and the Gga1/2-dependent, Golgi-to-vacuole pathway are required for the vacuolar delivery of Jen1.
source: Indeed, Jen1 localizes to the TGN after endocytosis, and both (i) the endosome-to-Golgi retrograde pathway and (ii) the Gga1/2-dependent, Golgi-to-vacuole pathway are required for the vacuolar delivery of Jen1, indicating a critical role for the TGN in transporter degradation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings in the discussion.

claim: The yeast TGN appears as a critical organelle for the post-endocytic sorting of transporters.
source: The yeast TGN therefore appears as a critical organelle for the post-endocytic sorting of transporters.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: This new level of regulation provides an opportunity to re-evaluate, after internalization, the commitment of transporters to the degradation pathway.
source: This new level of regulation provides an opportunity to re-evaluate, after internalization, the commitment of transporters to the degradation pathway.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings in the discussion.

claim: Upon glucose removal, internalized Jen1 recycles to the cell surface after it has reached the TGN.
source: Indeed, upon glucose removal, we show that internalized Jen1 recycles to the cell surface after it has reached the TGN (Figure 6; Figure 8, right panel).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings in the discussion.

claim: External signals can remodel transporter ubiquitylation at the TGN through the regulation of ART proteins, and therefore control transporter targeting towards the recycling or degradation pathways.
source: Here, we propose that external signals can remodel transporter ubiquitylation at the TGN through the regulation of ART proteins, and therefore control transporter targeting towards the recycling or degradation pathways.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed model in the discussion.

claim: The continuous presence of glucose is not only required to trigger Jen1 internalization, but also to maintain Jen1 in the endocytic pathway and prevent its recycling.
source: Therefore, the continuous presence of glucose is not only required to trigger Jen1 internalization, but also to maintain Jen1 in the endocytic pathway and prevent its recycling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: A glucose-induced recruitment of Rod1 to the TGN curtails Jen1 recycling and promotes its vacuolar sorting, leading to its degradation.
source: Here, we propose that a glucose-induced recruitment of the arrestin-related protein Rod1 to the TGN curtails Jen1 recycling and promotes its vacuolar sorting, leading to its degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed model in the discussion.

claim: Rod1 relocalization to the TGN relies on rapid glucose-induced changes in Rod1 post-translational modifications.
source: This re-localization relies on rapid glucose-induced changes in Rod1 post-translational modifications through a mechanism that we previously established (Becuwe et al., 2012b), and both are reversible upon glucose removal (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation and data.

claim: The use of the same machinery to regulate transporter trafficking at the plasma membrane and the TGN allows an integrated control of transporter sorting both during secretion and after endocytosis at the same location.
source: Noteworthy, the use of the same machinery to regulate transporter trafficking at the plasma membrane and the TGN also allows an integrated control of transporter sorting both during secretion and after endocytosis at the same location (Figure 7; Figure 8, middle panel).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the discussion.

claim: This may be critical to prevent neosynthesized cargoes transiting in the secretory pathway from reaching the cell surface in conditions that induce endocytosis.
source: This may be critical to prevent neosynthesized cargoes transiting in the secretory pathway from reaching the cell surface in conditions that induce endocytosis.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: The Bul1/Bul2 proteins may act at the TGN to control both sorting of neosynthesized Gap1 and Gap1 down-regulation.
source: Intriguingly, the ART-related proteins Bul1 and Bul2 were shown to control the sorting of neosynthesized Gap1 between the Golgi and the vacuole (Helliwell et al., 2001; Soetens et al., 2001; Risinger and Kaiser, 2008), and then later found to be involved in Gap1 down-regulation, suggestive of a role at the plasma membrane (Risinger and Kaiser, 2008; Merhi and André, 2012). In the light of our data, it appears likely that the Bul1/Bul2 proteins may in fact act at the TGN to control both of these sorting events.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the current findings and supported by citations.
